title: General Science — Physics, Chemistry, Biology & First Aid
why: Everyday science is the most predictable slice of the IPO GK paper: 2022 alone asked why the sky is blue, how a pressure cooker works, quinine for malaria, insulin, a skin bacterium and first aid for cardiac arrest. The questions are NCERT Class 6–10 level and mostly one-line facts, so a few focused tables (phenomenon → cause, name → formula, disease → cause, vitamin → deficiency) convert directly into marks.

lessons.title: Physics I — Light, lenses, eye defects and sound
lessons.body:
### Light — what causes what

| Phenomenon | Everyday example | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| Reflection | Mirror image, periscope | Light bounces off a surface |
| Refraction | Pencil looks bent in water; pool looks shallower; lens | Light changes speed/direction entering a new medium |
| Atmospheric refraction | Stars **twinkle** (planets don't); Sun visible ~2 min before actual sunrise and after sunset | Layers of air with different density |
| Total internal reflection (TIR) | **Diamond sparkles** (n ≈ 2.42, critical angle ≈ 24°), **optical fibre**, **mirage** in deserts/hot roads | Light goes from denser to rarer medium at angle > critical angle |
| Dispersion | **Rainbow**, prism spectrum (VIBGYOR) | Different colours bend by different amounts |
| Scattering (Rayleigh) | **Sky is blue**, sunrise/sunset **red**, danger lights are **red** | Scattering ∝ 1/λ⁴ → blue (short λ) scatters most, red least |
| Interference | Colours of **soap bubbles**, oil film on water | Waves reflected from two surfaces combine |
| Diffraction | Light bending round edges; CD rainbow | Waves spreading past obstacles |
| Polarisation | Polaroid sunglasses | Light vibrating in one plane |

> Sky on the **Moon** looks black — no atmosphere, so no scattering. Clouds look white because large droplets scatter all colours equally.

**Speed of light** ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s (fastest in vacuum). Sunlight takes about **8 min 20 s** to reach Earth; moonlight about 1.3 s.

### Mirrors and lenses

| Device | Used in | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Concave mirror | Shaving/make-up mirror, dentist's mirror, torch & vehicle **headlight reflectors**, solar cooker | Converges light; magnified upright image when object is close |
| Convex mirror | **Rear-view mirror** of vehicles, road-bend mirrors | Wider field of view, always erect diminished image |
| Plane mirror | Looking glass, periscope | Lateral inversion |
| Convex lens | Magnifying glass, camera, correcting **hypermetropia** | Converging |
| Concave lens | Correcting **myopia** | Diverging |

### Eye defects

| Defect | Can see | Image forms | Correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| Myopia (short-sight) | Near objects | In front of retina | **Concave** lens |
| Hypermetropia (long-sight) | Far objects | Behind retina | **Convex** lens |
| Presbyopia (old age) | Neither near work well | Ciliary muscles weaken | **Bifocal** lens |
| Astigmatism | Blurred in one direction | Irregular cornea | **Cylindrical** lens |
| Cataract | Cloudy vision | Eye lens becomes opaque | Surgery (lens replacement) |

Power of a lens P = 1/f (f in metres); unit **dioptre**; convex lens has +ve power, concave −ve.

### Sound

| Fact | Value / Note |
|---|---|
| Needs a medium? | **Yes** — cannot travel in vacuum (astronauts use radio) |
| Speed order | Solids > liquids > gases (steel ~5000+ m/s, water ~1500 m/s, air ~343 m/s at 20 °C, ~332 m/s at 0 °C) |
| Speed rises with | Temperature and humidity of air (not with pressure alone) |
| Audible range (humans) | **20 Hz – 20,000 Hz** |
| Infrasonic (< 20 Hz) | Earthquakes, elephants, whales |
| Ultrasonic (> 20 kHz) | **Bats**, dolphins, SONAR, ultrasound scan, cleaning |
| Pitch depends on | **Frequency** (female voice higher pitch) |
| Loudness depends on | **Amplitude**; measured in **decibel (dB)** |
| Quality / timbre | Waveform — lets us tell a violin from a flute |
| Echo | Needs reflecting surface ≥ **17.2 m** away (sound persists in ear ~0.1 s) |
| SONAR | Uses ultrasonic waves to find depth/submarines |
| Supersonic | Faster than sound; **Mach 1** = speed of sound; crossing it gives a **sonic boom** |

lessons.title: Physics II — Pressure, fluids, heat, electricity, units and instruments
lessons.body:
### Pressure and fluids

| Principle | Statement (one line) | Everyday use |
|---|---|---|
| Pressure = Force / Area | Less area → more pressure | Sharp knife cuts; nails pointed; wide straps on school bags; camels' broad feet on sand |
| Atmospheric pressure | ≈ 101.3 kPa = 76 cm of mercury at sea level | Drinking with a straw; **sudden fall in barometer → storm** |
| Boiling point vs pressure | Higher pressure → higher boiling point | **Pressure cooker** (water boils ~120 °C, cooks faster); on hills water boils **below 100 °C**, so cooking is slow |
| Pascal's law | Pressure on enclosed fluid is transmitted equally | Hydraulic lift, hydraulic brakes, hydraulic press |
| Archimedes' principle | Upthrust = weight of fluid displaced | Ships float; hydrometer, **lactometer**; a ship **rises** when it moves from river to sea (sea water is denser) |
| Bernoulli's principle | Faster flow → lower pressure | **Aeroplane lift**, roofs blown off in storms, atomiser/spray |
| Surface tension | Liquid surface acts like a stretched film | Raindrops are spherical; insects walk on water; soap/detergent **lowers** it |
| Capillarity | Liquid rises in narrow tubes | Oil in lamp wick, blotting paper, water in soil |
| Viscosity | Internal friction of fluid | Honey flows slower than water |

### Heat

| Idea | Key fact |
|---|---|
| Conduction | Through solids (metal spoon gets hot). Metals good conductors; wood, air poor |
| Convection | Through fluids by movement — **sea breeze by day, land breeze by night**, boiling water |
| Radiation | No medium needed — **Sun's heat reaches Earth by radiation** |
| Thermos flask | Vacuum stops conduction & convection; silvered walls stop radiation |
| Dark vs light colours | Black absorbs and emits best; wear **white** in summer |
| Scales | K = °C + 273; °F = 9/5 °C + 32; **−40 °C = −40 °F** |
| Body temperature | **37 °C = 98.6 °F ≈ 310 K** (clinical thermometer range 35–42 °C) |
| Anomalous expansion | Water is **densest at 4 °C**; ice floats, so lakes freeze from the top and fish survive |
| Latent heat | Steam at 100 °C burns more than water at 100 °C (extra latent heat) |
| Evaporation cools | Earthen pot (matka) keeps water cool; sweating cools body |

### Electricity & magnetism in the home

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| Household supply (India) | **230 V, 50 Hz AC** |
| Fuse | Wire of low melting point (tin–lead alloy), connected in **series** |
| Bulb filament | **Tungsten** (very high melting point ~3422 °C); bulb filled with inert gas (argon/nitrogen) |
| Heater/iron element | **Nichrome** (high resistance) |
| Earth wire | Green insulation; protects from shock |
| Electric motor | Electrical → mechanical energy |
| Generator / dynamo | Mechanical → electrical (Faraday's **electromagnetic induction**) |
| Transformer | Works only on **AC**; steps voltage up/down |
| Solar cell | Light → electrical |
| Microphone / loudspeaker | Sound → electrical / electrical → sound |

### SI units & odd units

| Quantity | Unit | Quantity | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Force | newton | Pressure | pascal |
| Work/energy | joule | Power | watt (1 HP = **746 W**) |
| Current | ampere | Resistance | ohm |
| Charge | coulomb | Frequency | hertz |
| Luminous intensity | candela | Magnetic flux | weber |
| Commercial energy | **kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J** | Temperature | kelvin |

| Odd unit | Measures |
|---|---|
| Light-year | **Distance** (≈ 9.46 × 10¹² km), not time |
| Parsec | Distance (astronomy) |
| Nautical mile | Distance at sea = 1.852 km |
| Knot | **Speed** of ships/aircraft (1 nautical mile per hour) |
| Fathom | **Depth** of water = 6 feet |
| Angstrom (Å) | Wavelength = 10⁻¹⁰ m |
| Decibel | Sound level |

### Instruments

| Instrument | Measures | Instrument | Measures |
|---|---|---|---|
| Barometer | Atmospheric pressure | Hygrometer | **Relative humidity** |
| Hydrometer | Density of liquids | **Lactometer** | Purity (density) of milk |
| Anemometer | Wind speed | Seismograph | Earthquake waves |
| Altimeter | Altitude | Pyrometer | Very high temperatures |
| Sphygmomanometer | Blood pressure | Tachometer | RPM of engines |
| Odometer | Distance travelled by vehicle | Manometer | Gas pressure |
| Ammeter | Current (in series) | Voltmeter | Potential difference (in parallel) |
| Galvanometer | Small currents | Audiometer | Hearing |

lessons.title: Chemistry — Common names, acids & bases, metals, alloys and pollutants
lessons.body:
### Common names → chemical names/formulas

| Common name | Chemical | Formula | Use / fact |
|---|---|---|---|
| Common salt | Sodium chloride | NaCl | Food, raw material for many chemicals |
| **Baking soda** | Sodium bicarbonate (hydrogen carbonate) | NaHCO₃ | Antacid, baking; **baking powder** = baking soda + tartaric acid |
| **Washing soda** | Sodium carbonate decahydrate | Na₂CO₃·10H₂O | Removes permanent hardness, glass making |
| Bleaching powder | Calcium oxychloride | CaOCl₂ | Disinfecting drinking water |
| **Plaster of Paris** | Calcium sulphate hemihydrate | CaSO₄·½H₂O | Sets into **gypsum** (CaSO₄·2H₂O) with water — fractures, statues |
| Quicklime / slaked lime | Calcium oxide / hydroxide | CaO / Ca(OH)₂ | Whitewash |
| Limestone, marble, chalk | Calcium carbonate | CaCO₃ | Marble corroded by acid rain (Taj Mahal "marble cancer") |
| Caustic soda / potash | Sodium / potassium hydroxide | NaOH / KOH | Soap making |
| Blue vitriol | Copper sulphate | CuSO₄·5H₂O | Fungicide |
| Green vitriol | Ferrous sulphate | FeSO₄·7H₂O | Iron supplement |
| Oil of vitriol | Sulphuric acid | H₂SO₄ | "King of chemicals" |
| Muriatic acid | Hydrochloric acid | HCl | Also in stomach |
| **Laughing gas** | Nitrous oxide | N₂O | Anaesthetic |
| **Dry ice** | Solid carbon dioxide | CO₂ | Refrigerant, stage fog |
| **Heavy water** | Deuterium oxide | D₂O | **Moderator** in nuclear reactors |
| Marsh gas | Methane | CH₄ | Main part of **CNG and biogas** |
| Potash alum | Potassium aluminium sulphate | K₂SO₄·Al₂(SO₄)₃·24H₂O | Water purification (coagulation), after-shave |
| Aqua regia | 3 HCl : 1 HNO₃ | — | Dissolves **gold & platinum** |
| Vinegar | Dilute acetic acid (~5–8 %) | CH₃COOH | Pickles |
| Rust | Hydrated ferric oxide | Fe₂O₃·xH₂O | Needs **both oxygen and water** |

**Fuels:** LPG = mainly **butane** (+ propane) — ethyl mercaptan added for smell; CNG = **methane**; water gas = CO + H₂; producer gas = CO + N₂.

### Acids, bases and pH

pH 0–14: < 7 acidic, 7 neutral, > 7 basic. Blood ≈ **7.4** (slightly basic); gastric juice ≈ 1.5–2 (HCl); milk ≈ 6.5; pure water 7.

| Natural acid | Found in | Natural acid | Found in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Citric | Lemon, orange | Lactic | Curd, sour milk |
| Tartaric | Tamarind, grapes | Acetic | Vinegar |
| Oxalic | Tomato, spinach | **Formic** | **Ant sting**, nettle leaves |
| Malic | Apple | Butyric | Rancid butter |
| Uric | Urine | Hydrochloric | Stomach |

- **Bee sting / ant sting** is acidic → rub **baking soda** (base). Wasp sting is alkaline → vinegar.
- **Antacid** for acidity: milk of magnesia Mg(OH)₂ or baking soda.
- Acid turns blue litmus red; base turns red litmus blue. Phenolphthalein is pink in bases.
- Curd forms when **Lactobacillus** converts milk sugar (lactose) to lactic acid.

### Metals, non-metals and alloys

| Record | Answer |
|---|---|
| Liquid metal at room temperature | **Mercury** (liquid non-metal: **bromine**) |
| Metal that melts in the palm | Gallium |
| Highest melting point metal | **Tungsten** (bulb filaments) |
| Lightest metal | Lithium (lightest element: hydrogen) |
| Best conductor of electricity | **Silver**, then copper |
| Most malleable & ductile | **Gold** |
| Most abundant metal in Earth's crust | **Aluminium** (most abundant element: **oxygen**) |
| Most abundant gas in air | **Nitrogen ~78 %**; oxygen ~21 %; argon ~0.93 %; CO₂ ~0.04 % |
| Stored in kerosene | Sodium, potassium (react violently with air/water) |
| Stored under water | White phosphorus |
| Hardest natural substance | Diamond (carbon); **graphite** (also carbon) is soft and conducts electricity — pencil "lead" |
| Pure gold | 24 carat; 22 carat ≈ 91.6 % gold |

| Alloy | Composition | Alloy | Composition |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Brass** | Copper + **Zinc** | **Bronze** | Copper + **Tin** |
| Stainless steel | Iron + chromium + nickel (+ C) | **German silver** | Cu + Zn + Ni (**no silver**) |
| Solder | Tin + lead | Amalgam | Any metal + **mercury** |

| Ore | Metal | Ore | Metal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bauxite | Aluminium | Haematite, magnetite | Iron |
| Galena | Lead | Cinnabar | Mercury |
| Zinc blende | Zinc | Chalcopyrite | Copper |

**Galvanisation** = coating iron with **zinc** to stop rusting. **Hard water**: Ca/Mg salts — temporary hardness (bicarbonates) removed by boiling; permanent (chlorides/sulphates) by washing soda. **Soap** = sodium/potassium salt of fatty acids (saponification). Noble gases: **neon** in advertising signs, **argon** in bulbs, **helium** in balloons and divers' breathing mix.

### Pollutant-linked diseases (favourite MCQ)

| Disease | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Minamata** disease | Mercury (Japan) |
| **Itai-itai** disease | Cadmium |
| Blue baby syndrome | Nitrate in water |
| Black-foot disease | Arsenic |
| Fluorosis | Excess fluoride |
| Bhopal gas tragedy (1984) | **Methyl isocyanate (MIC)** |

lessons.title: Biology I — Cell, human body systems, hormones and blood groups
lessons.body:
### The cell

| Part | Job / nickname |
|---|---|
| Cell discovered | **Robert Hooke (1665)** in cork; nucleus — Robert Brown (1831); living cells/microbes first seen — **Leeuwenhoek** |
| Cell theory | Schleiden & Schwann (1838–39) |
| Mitochondria | **Powerhouse** — makes ATP |
| Ribosome | Protein synthesis ("protein factory") |
| Lysosome | **Suicide bag** (digestive enzymes) |
| Golgi body | Packaging & secretion |
| Chloroplast | Photosynthesis (plants) |
| Cell wall | Plants — made of **cellulose** |
| Nucleus | Controls cell; contains DNA (double helix — **Watson & Crick, 1953**) |
| Human chromosomes | **46 (23 pairs)**; sex decided by the father's X or Y |
| Longest cell | Nerve cell (neuron) |

### Human body — record table

| Item | Answer |
|---|---|
| Largest organ | **Skin** |
| Largest gland / largest internal organ | **Liver** (makes bile) |
| Master gland | **Pituitary** |
| Longest bone | Femur (thigh) |
| Smallest bone | **Stapes** (middle ear) |
| Bones in adult | **206** (a newborn has ~300, many fuse) |
| Hardest substance | Tooth **enamel** |
| Normal BP | **120/80 mm Hg** |
| Resting heart rate | ~72 beats/min |
| Normal temperature | 37 °C / 98.6 °F |
| Blood volume | ~5–6 litres in adults |
| Blood pH | ~7.4 |

### Systems quick notes

| System | Key facts |
|---|---|
| Circulatory | Heart has **4 chambers**; pacemaker = **SA node**; circulation discovered by **William Harvey**; arteries carry blood away from heart (pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood) |
| Blood | RBCs carry O₂ via **haemoglobin (iron)**; life ~**120 days**; made in **bone marrow**; spleen = "graveyard of RBCs". WBCs fight infection; **platelets** help clotting (vitamin K needed) |
| Respiratory | Gas exchange in **alveoli** of lungs |
| Digestive | Saliva has **ptyalin (salivary amylase)** for starch; stomach: HCl + **pepsin** (proteins); **bile** (liver, stored in gall bladder) emulsifies fat — has no enzyme; most absorption in small intestine |
| Excretory | **Kidney** — unit is **nephron**; dialysis when kidneys fail |
| Nervous | **Cerebrum** = thinking, memory; **cerebellum** = balance & coordination; **medulla oblongata** = involuntary acts (breathing, heartbeat); neuron is the unit |
| Eye | **Retina** — rods (dim light), cones (colour); **cornea** is the part donated |

### Hormones

| Gland | Hormone | Deficiency/excess |
|---|---|---|
| Pancreas (islets of Langerhans, β-cells) | **Insulin** (lowers blood sugar) | Diabetes mellitus |
| Thyroid | Thyroxine (needs **iodine**) | Goitre, cretinism |
| Adrenal | **Adrenaline** — "fight or flight" / emergency hormone | — |
| Pituitary | Growth hormone | Dwarfism / gigantism |
| Pancreas is both | exocrine (digestive juice) and endocrine | |

### Blood groups

| Group | Antigen on RBC | Antibody in plasma | Can donate to | Can receive from |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | A | anti-B | A, AB | A, O |
| B | B | anti-A | B, AB | B, O |
| AB | A and B | none | AB only | **All** → **universal recipient** |
| O | none | anti-A and anti-B | **All** → **universal donor** | O only |

- ABO groups discovered by **Karl Landsteiner** (1900–01). **Rh factor** named after the **rhesus monkey** (Landsteiner & Wiener, 1940). O-negative is the true universal donor; AB-positive the universal recipient.
- Rh-negative mother + Rh-positive baby → risk in later pregnancies (erythroblastosis fetalis).

### Useful microbes

| Microbe | Role |
|---|---|
| *Lactobacillus* | Curd from milk |
| Yeast (*Saccharomyces*) | Bread rising, alcohol fermentation (releases CO₂) |
| *Rhizobium* | Nitrogen fixation in root nodules of **legumes** |
| *Penicillium* | Penicillin antibiotic |
| *Staphylococcus epidermidis* | Normal **harmless skin** bacterium (commensal); can infect catheters/implants |
| *E. coli* | Normal gut bacterium; used in genetic engineering |

lessons.title: Biology II — Diseases, vitamins, medicines and discoverers
lessons.body:
### Diseases and their causes

| Type | Disease | Organism | Vector / spread / test |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bacterial | **Tuberculosis** | *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* (Robert Koch, 1882) | Air; BCG vaccine; World TB Day 24 Mar |
| Bacterial | Leprosy | *Mycobacterium leprae* (Hansen) | Long contact |
| Bacterial | **Cholera** | *Vibrio cholerae* | Contaminated water |
| Bacterial | **Typhoid** | *Salmonella typhi* | Food/water; **Widal test** |
| Bacterial | Tetanus (lockjaw) | *Clostridium tetani* | Rusty wounds, soil |
| Bacterial | Diphtheria | *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* | Throat; DPT vaccine |
| Bacterial | Whooping cough | *Bordetella pertussis* | DPT vaccine |
| Bacterial | Plague | *Yersinia pestis* | **Rat flea** |
| Viral | AIDS | HIV | Blood, sex; **ELISA** test |
| Viral | **Dengue**, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever | Viruses | ***Aedes aegypti*** (day-biting) |
| Viral | Japanese encephalitis | Virus | *Culex* mosquito (pigs are hosts) |
| Viral | Polio, measles, mumps, rabies, hepatitis, influenza, chickenpox, COVID-19 | Viruses | Rabies from dog bite (hydrophobia) |
| Viral | Smallpox | Variola virus | **Eradicated (WHO, 1980)** |
| Protozoan | **Malaria** | ***Plasmodium*** | **Female *Anopheles*** mosquito |
| Protozoan | Kala-azar | *Leishmania donovani* | **Sandfly** |
| Protozoan | Sleeping sickness | *Trypanosoma* | **Tsetse fly** |
| Protozoan | Amoebic dysentery | *Entamoeba histolytica* | Water/food |
| Helminth | Filariasis (elephantiasis) | *Wuchereria bancrofti* | **Culex** mosquito |
| Fungal | Ringworm, athlete's foot | Fungi | Contact |
| Genetic | Haemophilia (bleeder's disease), colour blindness | X-linked | Mostly males affected |
| Genetic | Down syndrome | Trisomy 21 | Extra chromosome 21 |
| Genetic | Sickle-cell anaemia | Abnormal haemoglobin | — |

> Antibiotics act on **bacteria**, not viruses. India was certified **polio-free by WHO in March 2014** (last case January 2011).

### Vitamins & minerals

| Vitamin | Chemical name | Deficiency disease | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Retinol | **Night blindness**, xerophthalmia | Carrot, milk, fish-liver oil |
| B1 | Thiamine | **Beriberi** | Whole grains |
| B2 | Riboflavin | Cracked lips (cheilosis) | Milk, eggs |
| B3 | Niacin | **Pellagra** (3 Ds: dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia) | Groundnut, meat |
| B9 | Folic acid | Anaemia, neural-tube defects in foetus | Green leaves |
| B12 | Cobalamin (contains **cobalt**) | **Pernicious anaemia** | Animal foods only |
| C | Ascorbic acid | **Scurvy** (bleeding gums) | Amla, citrus — destroyed by heat |
| D | Calciferol | **Rickets** (children), osteomalacia (adults) | **Sunlight**, fish oil |
| E | Tocopherol | Reproductive problems; antioxidant | Vegetable oils |
| K | Phylloquinone | **Poor blood clotting** | Green leaves |

Fat-soluble: **A, D, E, K**; water-soluble: B-complex, C. Minerals: iron → anaemia; **iodine → goitre**; calcium → bones/teeth; fluorine → teeth (excess = fluorosis). Protein deficiency: **kwashiorkor**; protein + calorie deficiency: **marasmus**.

### Medicines, vaccines and discoverers

| Discovery | By | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Smallpox vaccine | **Edward Jenner (1796)** | First vaccine ("vacca" = cow) |
| Rabies vaccine, pasteurisation | **Louis Pasteur** (1885) | Germ theory |
| Penicillin | **Alexander Fleming (1928)** | First antibiotic, from *Penicillium* mould |
| Streptomycin | Selman Waksman | First drug against TB |
| Insulin | Banting & Best (1921) | Diabetes |
| Polio vaccine | **Jonas Salk** (injected, IPV); **Albert Sabin** (oral, OPV) | |
| BCG vaccine | Calmette & Guérin | Tuberculosis |
| Quinine | Bark of **cinchona** tree | Malaria |
| Artemisinin | Tu Youyou (Nobel 2015) | Malaria |
| Aspirin | Salicylic acid derivative (willow bark) | Pain, fever, blood thinner |
| Morphine | Opium poppy | Painkiller (analgesic) |
| Chloroform as anaesthetic | James Simpson | |
| X-rays | **W. C. Röntgen (1895)** | |
| ABO blood groups | Karl Landsteiner | |
| DNA double helix | Watson & Crick (1953) | |

| Medicine class | Does what |
|---|---|
| Analgesic | Relieves pain (aspirin, paracetamol) |
| Antipyretic | Reduces fever (paracetamol) |
| Antibiotic | Kills/inhibits bacteria |
| Antiseptic | Applied on living tissue (Dettol, iodine tincture, boric acid) |
| Disinfectant | Used on non-living surfaces (phenol, bleaching powder) |
| Antacid | Neutralises stomach acid |
| Tranquilliser | Reduces anxiety |

| Test / scan | For |
|---|---|
| ECG | Heart |
| EEG | Brain |
| MRI | Soft tissues using strong magnets (no X-rays) |
| CT scan | X-ray cross-sections |
| Widal | Typhoid |
| ELISA | HIV |

lessons.title: First aid basics
lessons.body:
### First aid — the exam-relevant basics

**First check:** **D-R-S-A-B-C** → **D**anger (make scene safe) → **R**esponse (tap, shout) → **S**end for help (call **112**/108 ambulance) → **A**irway (head-tilt, chin-lift) → **B**reathing (look, listen, feel ≤ 10 s) → **C**PR / Circulation.

| Emergency | Do | Don't |
|---|---|---|
| **Cardiac arrest** (unresponsive, not breathing normally) | Call for help and an **AED**; start **CPR**: **30 chest compressions : 2 rescue breaths**; rate **100–120/min**; depth **5–6 cm** in adults, centre of chest; untrained people give **hands-only CPR** | Don't wait for a pulse check if unsure; don't stop until help/AED arrives |
| Heart attack (conscious, chest pain) | Keep patient seated and calm, call ambulance; aspirin to chew if advised | Don't let the patient walk about |
| **Choking** (adult, cannot speak/cough) | **5 back blows + 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre)**, repeat | Don't do blind finger sweeps |
| **Burns** | Cool under **running water for ~20 minutes**; cover with cling film/clean cloth | **No ice, butter, toothpaste**; don't burst blisters |
| **Nosebleed** | Sit, **lean forward**, pinch the soft part of nose 10–15 min | Don't tilt the head back |
| Bleeding | **Direct pressure** with clean pad, raise the limb | Don't remove embedded objects |
| **Fracture** | Immobilise with a **splint**, support the limb | Don't try to straighten the bone |
| **Snakebite** | Keep calm and still, immobilise limb, remove rings, rush to hospital for **anti-snake venom (ASV)** | **No cutting, sucking, tight tourniquet**, or ice |
| Dog bite | Wash with soap and running water ~15 min; anti-rabies vaccine | Don't close the wound tightly |
| Heatstroke | Move to shade, loosen clothes, cool with water/fanning, sips of water if conscious | Don't give alcohol/caffeine |
| Fainting | Lay flat, **raise legs**, loosen tight clothing | Don't crowd the person |
| Unconscious but breathing | **Recovery position** (on the side) | Don't give food or water |
| Diarrhoea/dehydration | **ORS** (oral rehydration solution) | — |
| Electric shock | **Switch off supply** / use dry wooden stick first | Don't touch the victim directly |

### First-aid facts that get asked

| Fact | Answer |
|---|---|
| Founder of the Red Cross | **Henry Dunant** (1863, Geneva); first Nobel Peace Prize 1901 (shared) |
| World Red Cross Day | **8 May** (Dunant's birthday) |
| World First Aid Day | **Second Saturday of September** |
| AED | Automated External Defibrillator — gives a shock to restart normal rhythm |
| "Golden hour" | First hour after trauma, when treatment saves most lives |
| CPR full form | Cardio-Pulmonary Resuscitation |
| Heimlich manoeuvre | For choking (abdominal thrusts) |

> CPR numbers follow current resuscitation guidelines (AHA/ERC): 30:2, 100–120 per minute, 5–6 cm deep (as of September 2026).

examples.q: Type: 'Why does X happen?' (e.g. why do stars twinkle / why does a diamond sparkle / why is the sky blue?)
examples.solution:
Step 1: Identify the phenomenon family — bending (refraction), bouncing inside (total internal reflection), splitting (dispersion), spreading (scattering), colour bands (interference).
Step 2: Map it: twinkling → atmospheric refraction; diamond/optical fibre/mirage → total internal reflection; rainbow → dispersion (+ TIR inside drops); blue sky/red sunset → scattering; soap-bubble colours → interference.
Step 3: Eliminate options from other families.
Answer: pick the family, not the fancy word.
examples.shortcut: Sky, sunset, danger light = scattering. Sparkle, fibre, mirage = TIR. Twinkle, early sunrise = atmospheric refraction.

examples.q: Type: Common name ↔ chemical formula (e.g. 'The chemical formula of Plaster of Paris is…')
examples.solution:
Step 1: Recall the parent compound family — calcium sulphate for PoP/gypsum, sodium carbonate/bicarbonate for washing/baking soda.
Step 2: Check water of crystallisation: PoP = ½H₂O, gypsum = 2H₂O, washing soda = 10H₂O, blue vitriol = 5H₂O.
Step 3: Reject options that swap Na₂CO₃ (washing) and NaHCO₃ (baking).
Answer: the option with the correct parent AND correct water count.
examples.shortcut: 'Baking has H' — baking soda is the one with H (NaHCO₃).

examples.q: Type: Disease ↔ cause / vector matching (e.g. 'Kala-azar is spread by…')
examples.solution:
Step 1: Classify the disease: bacterial, viral, protozoan, helminth.
Step 2: Recall the vector: Anopheles = malaria; Aedes = dengue/chikungunya/Zika/yellow fever; Culex = filaria/Japanese encephalitis; sandfly = kala-azar; tsetse = sleeping sickness; rat flea = plague.
Step 3: Watch for the 'female Anopheles' qualifier — only females bite.
Answer: sandfly.
examples.shortcut: 'A-D' — Aedes → Dengue; 'A-M' — Anopheles → Malaria; 'C-F' — Culex → Filaria.

examples.q: Type: Vitamin ↔ deficiency (e.g. 'Pellagra is caused by deficiency of…')
examples.solution:
Step 1: Recall the table: A night blindness, B1 beriberi, B3 pellagra, B12 pernicious anaemia, C scurvy, D rickets, K clotting.
Step 2: If the question gives the chemical name (niacin, thiamine, calciferol), convert it first.
Answer: Vitamin B3 (niacin).
examples.shortcut: 'Be-Be-ri' — B1 for Beriberi; 'C for Scurvy, C for Citrus'.

examples.q: Type: 'Which instrument measures…' (e.g. relative humidity, purity of milk, blood pressure)
examples.solution:
Step 1: Split the word: hygro = moisture, hydro = water/liquid, lacto = milk, anemo = wind, seismo = earthquake, pyro = fire/heat, sphygmo = pulse.
Step 2: Match the prefix to the quantity.
Answer: hygrometer = humidity; lactometer = milk; sphygmomanometer = blood pressure.
examples.shortcut: Greek/Latin prefix almost always gives it away.

examples.q: Type: First-aid procedure (e.g. 'Correct first aid for a minor burn is…')
examples.solution:
Step 1: Remember first aid follows current guidelines — the 'grandmother remedies' (ice, butter, toothpaste, sucking snake venom, tilting head back for nosebleed) are always the WRONG options.
Step 2: Pick the option with cool running water / direct pressure / immobilisation / calling for help.
Answer: hold under cool running water for about 20 minutes.
examples.shortcut: If an option sounds like a home remedy, it is the trap.

traps: Mirage and diamond sparkle are total internal reflection, not simple refraction or scattering; twinkling of stars is atmospheric refraction, not scattering.
Myopia (short-sight) is corrected by a CONCAVE lens and hypermetropia by a CONVEX lens — many swap them. Rear-view mirror is CONVEX; shaving mirror and headlight reflector are CONCAVE.
Light-year measures DISTANCE, knot measures SPEED, fathom measures DEPTH — options often offer 'time' for light-year.
Baking soda (NaHCO₃) vs washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O); brass (Cu+Zn) vs bronze (Cu+Tin); German silver contains NO silver.
Universal DONOR is O; universal RECIPIENT is AB. Bile has no digestive enzyme; largest gland is the liver, not the pancreas.
Dengue is spread by Aedes (day-biting), malaria by FEMALE Anopheles, filaria and Japanese encephalitis by Culex; malaria is caused by a protozoan (Plasmodium), not a virus or bacterium.

practice.q: Which phenomenon is responsible for the twinkling of stars?
practice.explanation:
Starlight passes through air layers of changing density, so its path keeps shifting — atmospheric refraction. Planets are nearer (disc-like) and do not twinkle.
Hook: Stars twinkle, planets don't — both lie in the refracting atmosphere.

practice.q: Optical fibres used in telecommunication work on the principle of
practice.explanation:
Light keeps reflecting totally inside the glass core, so it travels long distances with little loss.
Hook: Fibre, diamond, mirage — the TIR trio.

practice.q: The colours seen on a thin film of oil spread on a wet road are due to
practice.explanation:
Light reflected from the top and bottom surfaces of the thin film interferes; different thicknesses reinforce different colours. Same reason as soap-bubble colours.
Hook: Thin film = interference.

practice.q: A person who can see nearby objects clearly but not distant ones should use
practice.explanation:
That is myopia (short-sightedness): the image forms in front of the retina; a diverging (concave) lens corrects it.
Hook: Myopia → Minus lens (concave).

practice.q: Which type of mirror is used as the rear-view mirror in vehicles?
practice.explanation:
A convex mirror always gives an erect, diminished image and a wider field of view.
Hook: Convex = 'see more' of the road behind.

practice.q: Sound waves with frequency above 20,000 Hz are called ultrasonic. Which of the following does NOT use ultrasonic waves?
practice.explanation:
Earthquake waves recorded by a seismograph are low-frequency (infrasonic range), not ultrasonic. Bats, SONAR and medical ultrasound all use ultrasonic waves.
Hook: Quakes and elephants rumble low (infrasonic); bats squeak high (ultrasonic).

practice.q: In which medium does sound travel fastest?
practice.explanation:
Speed of sound: solids > liquids > gases (steel ~5000+ m/s, water ~1500 m/s, air ~343 m/s). It cannot travel in vacuum at all.
Hook: Sound loves solids; light loves vacuum.

practice.q: Cooking is difficult at high altitudes because
options: There is less oxygen for the fuel to burn
Low atmospheric pressure lowers the boiling point of water
Low atmospheric pressure raises the boiling point of water
Water evaporates faster in cold air
practice.explanation:
Lower air pressure on mountains means water boils below 100 °C, so food gets less heat. A pressure cooker does the opposite (raises the boiling point).
Hook: Less pressure, lower boil.

practice.q: A ship moving from a river into the sea will
options: Sink or rise depending on its speed
practice.explanation:
Sea water is denser than river water, so less volume needs to be displaced to balance the ship's weight (Archimedes' principle) — the ship rises.
Hook: Salty sea holds you higher.

practice.q: Hydraulic brakes in automobiles work on
practice.explanation:
Pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions — Pascal's law. Also used in hydraulic lifts and presses.
Hook: Pascal = Press (hydraulic press, brakes, lift).

practice.q: Which of the following is a unit of distance?
practice.explanation:
A light-year is the distance light travels in a year (≈ 9.46 × 10¹² km). Knot = speed, decibel = sound level, kWh = energy.
Hook: Light-YEAR sounds like time but measures distance.

practice.q: The instrument used to measure relative humidity of air is
practice.explanation:
Hygro = moisture. Hydrometer measures density of liquids, barometer air pressure, anemometer wind speed.
Hook: HYGrometer = HYGiene of air's moisture — don't confuse with HYDRometer (liquids).

practice.q: At what temperature do the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales show the same reading?
practice.explanation:
Put C = F in F = 9C/5 + 32 → C = 9C/5 + 32 → −4C/5 = 32 → C = −40.
Hook: −40 is where the two scales shake hands.

practice.q: Why is the filament of an electric bulb made of tungsten?
options: It is the cheapest metal available
It has a very low resistance
It is the best conductor of electricity
It has a very high melting point
practice.explanation:
Tungsten melts at about 3422 °C, the highest of all metals, so it can glow white-hot without melting.
Hook: Tungsten = Tough at high Temperature.

practice.q: The chemical name of washing soda is
practice.explanation:
Washing soda = Na₂CO₃·10H₂O. Baking soda = NaHCO₃, bleaching powder = CaOCl₂, caustic soda = NaOH.
Hook: Washing needs lots of water — 10 H₂O.

practice.q: Plaster of Paris hardens on mixing with water because it changes into
practice.explanation:
CaSO₄·½H₂O (PoP) + 1½ H₂O → CaSO₄·2H₂O (gypsum), which sets hard — used for plasters on fractures.
Hook: PoP drinks water and turns back into gypsum.

practice.q: Which gas is the main constituent of CNG and biogas?
practice.explanation:
CNG is compressed natural gas, mostly methane; biogas is ~50–75 % methane. LPG is mainly butane (+ propane).
Hook: CNG and biogas = Methane; LPG = Butane.

practice.q: Aqua regia, which can dissolve gold, is a mixture of
options: Concentrated H₂SO₄ and HNO₃ in the ratio 1 : 1
Concentrated H₂SO₄ and HCl in the ratio 1 : 3
Concentrated HCl and HNO₃ in the ratio 3 : 1
Concentrated HNO₃ and HCl in the ratio 3 : 1
practice.explanation:
Aqua regia ('royal water') = 3 parts hydrochloric acid + 1 part nitric acid; it dissolves gold and platinum.
Hook: 'Three Hail One Nitric' — 3 HCl : 1 HNO₃.

practice.q: Which acid is present in an ant sting?
practice.explanation:
Ants (Latin formica) inject formic acid; rubbing a mild base like baking soda relieves the pain.
Hook: FORMica = ant → FORMic acid.

practice.q:
Match the natural substance with the acid it contains: (P) Tamarind (Q) Curd (R) Tomato (S) Vinegar
1. Lactic acid 2. Acetic acid 3. Tartaric acid 4. Oxalic acid
practice.explanation:
Tamarind – tartaric; curd – lactic; tomato – oxalic; vinegar – acetic.
Hook: TAmarind = TArtaric; Lactic = Lassi/curd.

practice.q: Brass is an alloy of
practice.explanation:
Brass = Cu + Zn; bronze = Cu + Sn (tin); German silver = Cu + Zn + Ni.
Hook: Brass has Zinc — 'BZ'; BronzE has tin.

practice.q: Which of the following metals is kept immersed in kerosene?
practice.explanation:
Sodium (and potassium) react vigorously with oxygen and moisture, so they are stored under kerosene. White phosphorus is stored under water.
Hook: Na naps in kerosene.

practice.q: The most abundant element in the Earth's crust is
practice.explanation:
Crust order: oxygen (~46 %) > silicon > aluminium > iron. Aluminium is the most abundant METAL.
Hook: 'OSAI' — Oxygen, Silicon, Aluminium, Iron.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Graphite is a good conductor of electricity.
2. Diamond and graphite are both allotropes of carbon.
3. Diamond is used as a moderator in nuclear reactors.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
practice.explanation:
Graphite conducts (free electrons); both are carbon allotropes. Moderators are heavy water or graphite — not diamond. So 1 and 2 only.
Hook: Graphite = pencil + conductor + moderator; diamond = only hard and sparkly.

practice.q: Galvanisation of iron means coating it with
practice.explanation:
A zinc layer protects iron from rusting even if scratched (zinc corrodes first). Tin-plating is used for food cans.
Hook: Galvanised = Zinc-ised.

practice.q: 'Itai-itai' disease, first reported in Japan, is caused by chronic poisoning from
practice.explanation:
Itai-itai ('ouch-ouch') came from cadmium-polluted rice water in Toyama; Minamata disease came from mercury.
Hook: Itai-itai = Cadmium ('ouch' from bones); Minamata = Mercury (both M).

practice.q: Which cell organelle is known as the 'suicide bag' of the cell?
practice.explanation:
Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes that can break down the cell's own parts when it is damaged.
Hook: Lysis = breaking → Lysosome self-destructs.

practice.q: The smallest bone in the human body is found in the
practice.explanation:
The stapes (stirrup) in the middle ear is the smallest bone; the femur is the longest.
Hook: Stapes = Small, Stirrup, in the ear.

practice.q: A person with blood group O can receive blood from a donor of group
practice.explanation:
Group O plasma has both anti-A and anti-B antibodies, so O can receive only from O. (O can donate to everyone.)
Hook: O gives to all but takes only O.

practice.q: Which of the following is the correct pair of vitamin and deficiency disease?
practice.explanation:
B1 (thiamine) → beriberi. Rickets = vitamin D, scurvy = vitamin C, pellagra = B3 (niacin); vitamin A → night blindness.
Hook: B1 = Beri-Beri (two Bs).

practice.q: Kala-azar is transmitted by
practice.explanation:
Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) is caused by Leishmania donovani and spread by sandflies. Tsetse spreads sleeping sickness.
Hook: Kala-azar in the Sand.

practice.q: Which disease is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae?
practice.explanation:
Cholera spreads by contaminated water and causes severe watery diarrhoea; ORS is the first-line treatment.
Hook: Vibrio → Cholera; Salmonella → typhoid.

practice.q: Which part of the human brain maintains balance and coordinates voluntary movements?
practice.explanation:
Cerebellum = balance and posture; cerebrum = thinking and memory; medulla = involuntary actions such as breathing and heartbeat.
Hook: CereBELLum keeps the body balanced like a bell.

practice.q: Who developed the first vaccine against smallpox?
practice.explanation:
Jenner (1796) used cowpox material; the word vaccine comes from Latin vacca (cow). Pasteur made the rabies vaccine; Fleming discovered penicillin; Koch found the TB bacterium.
Hook: Jenner → first 'Jab'.

practice.q: Which hormone is called the 'emergency' or 'fight-or-flight' hormone?
practice.explanation:
Adrenaline from the adrenal glands raises heart rate, blood sugar and alertness in danger.
Hook: Adrenaline rush = fight or flight.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Bile is produced by the gall bladder.
2. Bile contains no digestive enzyme.
3. Pepsin acts on proteins in the stomach.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
practice.explanation:
Bile is PRODUCED by the liver and only STORED in the gall bladder, so 1 is wrong. Bile emulsifies fat but has no enzyme; pepsin digests proteins in the stomach.
Hook: Liver makes, gall bladder stores.

practice.q: Root nodules of leguminous plants such as pea and gram contain bacteria that
practice.explanation:
Rhizobium in root nodules converts atmospheric N₂ into compounds plants can use, which is why pulses enrich the soil.
Hook: Rhizobium in Roots — nitrogen for free.

practice.q: While giving CPR to an adult in cardiac arrest, the recommended ratio of chest compressions to rescue breaths is
practice.explanation:
Current guidelines (AHA 2025 / ERC 2025, as of September 2026): 30 compressions then 2 breaths, at 100–120 compressions per minute, 5–6 cm deep. Untrained rescuers may give hands-only CPR.
Hook: '30-2, stay alive'.

practice.q: What is the correct first aid for a person with a nosebleed?
options: Sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose
Blow the nose hard to clear the clot
Put ice on the back of the neck and tilt the head back
Lie flat and tilt the head back
practice.explanation:
Leaning forward stops blood running down the throat; pinch the soft part of the nose for 10–15 minutes. Tilting the head back is the classic wrong answer.
Hook: Nosebleed → lean FORWARD, not back.

practice.q: Which of the following is the RIGHT first-aid step for a snakebite?
options: Keep the victim calm and still, immobilise the limb and take them to hospital for anti-venom
Apply ice to the bite and let the victim walk to hospital
Cut the wound and suck out the venom
Tie a tight tourniquet above the bite to stop blood flow
practice.explanation:
Movement spreads venom; cutting, sucking, tight tourniquets and ice cause harm. Immobilise and get anti-snake venom (ASV) quickly.
Hook: Snakebite — Still, Splint, Shift to hospital.
